content.text:
I submitted **holistic**, with confidence 0.93. I used 24 of the 60 budget: 2 for training and 22 for tests.

**Design:** I trained the learner on only two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L4-S2-M2. Then I tested tasks where the two hypotheses predict opposite results:
- **Recombined tasks (L4-S1-M1, L1-S2-M2):** every rule in them had already been trained, but their responses match the trained tasks on 0% of inputs. L4 gives the opposite answer to L1, and motors M1 and M2 never press the same button. A part-based learner should find these cheap.
- **Novel but similar tasks (L2-S3-M3, L2-S4-M3):** all three rules are new, but their responses match L1-S1-M1 on 56% of inputs. A holistic learner should find these cheap.

**Results (examples needed to reach criterion):**

| Task type | Samples | Mean |
|---|---|---|
| Recombined, no new rules, 0% match | 40, 31, 46, 47, 63, 38, 64, 38 | ~46 |
| All rules new, 56% match | 2, 36, 23, 9, 22, 21, 24, 6 | ~18 |
| All rules new, ~19% match (L3-S3-M3, for comparison) | 54, 37, 28 | ~40 |
| Already-trained task (L1-S1-M1) | 20, 13 | ~17 |

Learning cost followed how similar a task's responses were to the trained tasks, not how many of its rules were new. The recombined tasks cost about as much as a new, dissimilar task. The similar tasks with all-new rules were nearly as cheap as the trained task itself. That is the opposite of what the part-based learner predicts. The gap between the two main groups is large compared with the noise (roughly t ≈ 4.7 with 8 samples each), so I stopped there rather than spend more budget.
